title: Retained austenite grain size as a strength-plasticity relationship indicator in Al-alloyed medium-Mn steel processed by intercritical annealing
abstract: Although most studies focus on the impact of the fraction of retained austenite (RA) on the relationship between strength and plasticity, this research explores the influence of the mechanical stability of RA, which is primarily affected by its grain size. To investigate this, samples of 5% Mn steel with varying fractions of RA, as well as different sizes and concentrations of carbon (C) and manganese (Mn), were produced by adjusting the soaking time during intercritical annealing (IA) between 1 and 300 min at a temperature of 680 °C. The mechanical properties of the samples were evaluated using static tensile tests. Detailed microstructural analyses were conducted before and after deformation through hardness tests, X-ray diffraction measurements (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images, TEM-EDS microanalysis, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) phase and orientation maps. Additionally, thermodynamic calculations were used to supplement the experimental findings. The results suggest that both chemical enrichment and grain size reduction have comparable effects on stabilizing the RA. The wide variation of RA grain sizes from 0.02 to 0.15 μm3 promotes a gradual and continuous martensitic transformation under strain throughout the entire strain range, leading to a uniform elongation exceeding 19% in the steel analyzed. However, the presence of an appropriate average size of RA (from ∼0.07 to ∼0.11 μm3) is crucial because grains smaller than ∼0.02 μm3 impede martensitic transformation, while coarse grains characterized by a volume greater than ∼0.13 μm3 result in significant transformation in an early stage of deformation.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The strength and plastic properties of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) that are currently being developed rely significantly on the presence of retained austenite (RA) in the microstructure, in addition to the matrix phase [ 1 , 2 ]. The presence of RA significantly improves strain hardening and thus simultaneously improves ultimate tensile strength (UTS), uniform elongation (UEl), and total elongation (TEl) by the strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT). Three main types of heat treatment can be identified for medium-Mn steels, resulting in different matrix compositions and fractions of RA [ 3 , 4 ]: (i) austempering (bainitic matrix), (ii) quenching and partitioning (martensitic matrix), and (iii) IA (ferritic matrix). Among them, IA allows production of the highest fraction of RA (usually 20%–50%) in the microstructure, in a simple and cost-effective one-stage annealing in the A c1 –A c3  temperature range [ 5 , 6 ]. RA properties can be widely tailored by two main parameters of the IA process – (i) annealing temperature and (ii) soaking time. They allow control over the RA fraction and stability by influencing austenite formation, grain growth, and partitioning of selected alloying elements, particularly C and Mn.

Scientists frequently dedicate their efforts to achieving the maximum achievable fraction of (RA) that remains stable at room temperature (RT) [ 7–9 ]. However, a high fraction of RA is not a sufficient factor to ensure high mechanical performance. An equal or even more important factor is its stability, which controls the SIMT starting point and its kinetics. The stability of RA depends on many factors [ 10 ] including: (i) chemical composition [ 11 , 12 ], (ii) morphology [ 5 ], (iii) grain size [ 13 ], (iv) strength of surrounding phases [ 14 ] (v) or even crystallographic texture [ 15 ].

`The initial method for achieving chemical stabilization of (RA) in AHSS relied on C alloying. However, it is necessary to keep the C content at a relatively low level to ensure good weldability. As a result, steels intended for single IA are supplemented with the addition of Mn. In the case of medium-Mn steels, the Mn content typically falls in the range of 5%–12% [ 5 ]. The distribution of C and Mn and its resulting chemical composition in RA have been extensively studied [ 5 , 16–18 ]. However, to achieve a gradual SIMT effect and consequently enhance strain hardening throughout the entire deformation range, it is crucial to consider a factor that differentiates the mechanical stability of austenite. In this case, the martensitic transformation begins from the least stable austenite grains and progresses towards the most stable ones, ensuring a continuous transformation. It is hypothesized that the size of the RA grain may play a role as this differentiating factor. The stability of RA increases with a decrease in its size [ 19 ], which in turn influences the C and Mn diffusion paths during partitioning (chemical stabilization) and increases the number of martensite nuclei needed to obtain a given martensite fraction. The latter is caused by RA boundaries acting as obstacles to martensitic laths growth. The effect of the grain size of RA on mechanical stability has not been extensively studied [ 19–21 ], and its direct influence on the plasticity of medium-Mn steels has not investigated.

This paper specifically investigates the plasticity of steel, emphasizing the role of mechanical stability of RA rather than its fraction within the microstructure. The primary focus is on understanding the influence of RA grain size, as it is believed to be the main factor affecting the local stability of austenite, thereby enabling a gradual SIMT effect.

For the investigations, 4.5 mm thick hot-rolled medium-Mn steel with chemical composition presented in  Table 1 
                       was used. The detailed description of the chemical composition, design, and the production process is available in our previous work [ 22 ]. The steel was supplied by the Institute for Ferrous Metallurgy (Gliwice, Poland). The initial microstructure was composed of martensite due to increased hardenability [ 23 ] caused by the addition of Mn.

The sub-size tensile samples with 40 mm gauge length, 6 mm width and 2.5 mm thickness were machined from the initial steel plate along the rolling direction, and subsequently intercritically soaked at 680 °C for times ranging from 1 to 300 min under argon atmosphere using Nabertherm LT15/12/P330 muffle furnace. The heating time to the soaking temperature in the used furnace was determined using a PCE-T390 datalogger equipped with a K-type thermocouple placed in the middle of the sample thickness. These measurements were made to precisely soak the samples at a constant temperature. The final cooling was performed in water. The wide soaking time variation was applied to obtain different fractions, size and chemical stability of RA in each sample. The tensile properties of obtained materials were determined according to ASTM  E8  standard [ 24 ] in uniaxial static tensile tests using Zwick/Roell Z100 testing machine equipped with an extensometer at a nominal strain rate of 10 −3  s −1 . At least three tests were performed for each sample to verify the repeatability of the test. The selected samples (soaked for 1, 15 and 300 min) were also examined using interrupted tensile tests. In order to examine the variations over soaking time and assess their impact on the strength-plasticity behavior, each sample underwent a series of tests using various methods in the pre- and post-deformation (UEl and TEl) conditions. The TEl region is defined as the region within the neck of the sample, located approximately 1 mm from the fracture point of the sample, which has a local elongation of about 60%. The hardness was evaluated using a Vickers microhardness tester FB-700 at a load of 1 kgf. Ten measurements for each sample were taken, and after discarding the outliers, the mean hardness was calculated from the remaining values. The steel's microstructure was investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). SEM observations were performed using the JEOL JSM-7200F microscope equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer EDAX Hikari Plus EBSD detector. EBSD measurements were performed with SEM operating at 20 kV and a probe current of ∼2.5 nA. The samples were tilted at 70° and observed at a working distance of 15 mm. EBSD mapping has been performed in a hexagonal scan grid on 40 × 40 μm 2  areas at step sizes of 50 nm. OIM-TSL® data analysis software v.7.31 was used for data processing. A two-step cleanup procedure was performed. The grain conditions were set at a tolerance angle of 5° and a minimum size of 5 pixels. Points with a confidence index <0.1 were removed from the calculations as dubious. Since the microstructure of the investigated samples exhibited a lath-like morphology, the typical approach to grain size characterization by average diameter calculation was not appropriate. As the observed thicknesses of RA grains in the investigated samples did not show significant discrepancies, it was assumed that both the thickness and the width of RA were similar. The surfaces of the samples for metallographic and XRD investigations were prepared using a standard procedure. This involved grinding with SiC paper up to a 2000 grit, polishing with diamond pastes of 3 and 1 μm grain sizes, and final polishing with 35 nm colloidal silica (OPS). These steps were taken to achieve a flat surface with minimal deformation. For SEM observations samples were etched using 3% nital for ∼4 s at RT.

sections.heading: Microstructure and austenite stability
paragraphs:
The microstructural changes in samples after different intercritical soaking times and subsequent tensile tests are shown in SEM micrographs in  Fig. 1 
                         , and in EBSD maps in  Fig. 2 
                         . The microstructures of intercritically annealed samples exhibited lath-like morphologies regardless of the soaking time ( Fig. 1 a,c,e and  Fig. 2 a,c,e). The images are typical for hot rolled and intercritically annealed steel, as newly forming austenite inherits morphology from parent martensite [ 22 ]. RA may be distinguished in SEM images ( Fig. 1 ) by bright and “smooth” homogeneous appearance. The progress of the soaking is accompanied by growth and thickening of RA laths ( Fig. 1  a,c,e). Combinations of image quality (IQ) and phase (P) maps indicate that RA formed and grew along prior martensite lath boundaries ( Fig. 2 a,c,e) surrounding the grains of alpha (ferrite/tempered martensite) phase. Subfigures b,d and e in  Figs. 1 and 2  show the post deformation microstructures, which were sectioned from the UEl areas of tensile samples. Tensile deformation of the sample soaked for 1 min does not significantly affect the microstructure ( Fig. 1 b). Identification of transformed austenitic grains poses a significant challenge, as they are not easily discernible. Even the elongation of grains along the rolling direction is challenging to observe, primarily because both the matrix and the RA exhibit a highly lamellar morphology. The progress of soaking time results in a more visible martensitic transformation of RA in microstructures after tensile tests ( Fig. 1 d and f). In the sample soaked for 15 min and then subjected to tensile testing, the nital etching revealed that some areas of RA grains were characterized by rough and heterogeneous morphologies, characteristic of martensite in the structures. The number of RA grains exhibiting transformed areas is minor. The martensite in the sample soaked for 15 min at 680 °C is visible in the central part of RA grains [ 30 ], which is shown in higher magnification using TEM micrographs presented in  Fig. 3 
                         . Such tendency is related to the differentiated stability of RA which is caused by an inhomogeneous C and Mn enrichment of austenite after IA which was observed for this steel in earlier investigations [ 31 ].

The concentrations of C and Mn in RA depend directly on the diffusion path of these elements during heat treatment. Areas of the gamma phase adjacent to the alpha phase are usually more strongly enriched in alloying elements that stabilize austenite. This tendency is even stronger if the RA is adjacent to coarse ferritic grains and is caused by significantly faster diffusion of C and Mn in ferrite than in austenite [ 32 ]. Rapid depletion of even large ferrite grains into Mn and C occurs. However, these elements accumulate close to the austenite grain boundary, causing their stronger stabilization, which was confirmed by other researchers [ 17 ]. The TEM results also reveal a high dislocation density in both ferrite and RA. In the tensile sample soaked for 300 min, the transformed grains already constituted the majority of the initial RA fraction ( Fig. 1 f).

Some grains of RA in sample soaked for 300 min are completely transformed, whereas the others undergo fragmentation. The individual regions visible in  Fig. 1f and 2 f show a different degree of martensitic transformation, probably related to the crystallographic orientation and the grain orientation in relation to the tensile axis. De Knijf et al. [ 33 ] observed that RA grains with the main axis more perpendicular to the tensile direction seem to be more susceptible to martensitic transformation than grains that are parallel. Similar phenomena were observed in  Fig. 2 b,d,f. The tendency to increase the fraction of grains transformed to martensite during deformation was observed in SEM images ( Fig. 1 ). In samples subjected to longer soaking times, deformation promoted more intense martensitic transformation.

Table 2 
                          shows the chemical composition of RA after soaking at 680 °C for different times. As the fraction of RA increases with soaking time, its C enrichment decreases which is caused by fast diffusion of C, as reported by Král et al. [ 34 ]. On the other hand, the Mn enrichment of austenite increases with the progress of soaking despite increasing fraction of this phase, which is related to the very slow diffusion of this element in austenite [ 34 ]. The standard deviation of chemical composition measurements in RA for different areas is 0.03 wt% for C and 0.1 wt% for Mn, respectively. The low standard deviation values indicate the relatively homogeneous chemical composition of the investigated RA fraction.

The calculated mean RA grain volume ( Fig. 4 a) does not exceed 0.2 μm 3  in any variants of soaking time tested. A very rapid increase in relative grain size is observed as the soaking progresses from about 0.018 μm 3  after 1 min to almost 0.16 μm 3  after 300 min. The mean grain size of RA is characterized by a high standard deviation value, which increases for samples with longer soaking times and reaches 0.08 μm 3  for the sample soaked for 300 min. This is because the RA size is determined on the basis of the average grain volume of this phase, but it is a desirable result because of the need to indicate the impact of different RA grain sizes on the SIMT effect.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          shows the mechanical properties of samples soaked for different durations at 680 °C: (a-c) results of tensile tests, and (d) hardness of material after heat treatment, and of samples after tensile tests in UEl and TEl region. The stress - strain tensile curves of the investigated steel after different intercritical soaking are presented in  Fig. 5 a. The progress of intercritical soaking has a significant impact on the mechanical behavior of steel. As the soaking time increases, the plasticity initially experiences an increase ( Fig. 5 b). The UEl increases from 13.5% for the sample soaked for 1 min up to 19.2% for the sample soaked for 15 min, which was the maximum value among all tested time variants. The TEl increases from 18% for the sample soaked for 1 min up to 29% for the sample soaked for 60 min. However, the UEl of this sample reaches only 17% despite the RA fraction being higher by ∼6% than in the case of the sample soaked for 15 min. With a further increase in the soaking time, the plasticity decreases slightly to UEl of 16.4% and TEl of 26.5% for the sample soaked for 300 min. This result shows that the plasticity of intercritically annealed steel does not depend only on the fraction of RA in their microstructure. The results of the samples tensile tests of the tested showed high compliance and repeatability, which is confirmed by the small standard deviations of the measurements visible on the bars in  Fig. 4 b and c.

In terms of the strength of the intercritically annealed samples ( Fig. 5 c), three continuous trends with the progress of soaking: (i) significant decrease of yield strength (YS) from 860 MPa for the sample soaked for the 1 min to 590 MPa for sample soaked for 300 min, caused by martensite tempering and RA formation and coarsening; (ii) gradual increase in strain hardening increase (which is expressed by the UTS – YS value) from 80 MPa for the sample soaked for the 1 min to 300 MPa for sample soaked for 300 min related to an increasing fraction of transformed RA (SIMT effect); (iii) slight decrease in UTS from 940 MPa for the sample soaked 1 min to 890 MPa for the sample soaked for 300 min, which is a result of the decrease in YS for longer soaked samples and stronger strain hardening caused by more intense martensitic transformation. It is caused by an increase in the RA fraction and a decrease in its stability ( Fig. 4 b) for longer soaked samples.

The hardness of the nondeformed samples ( Fig. 5 d) shows a similar tendency as YS values; it decreases from 320 HV1 for the sample soaked for the 1 min to 280 HV1 for sample soaked for 300 min. Hardness of samples after the tensile tests is significantly higher and reaches a peak value for sample soaked for 60 min (380 HV1 in the UEl region and 420 HV1 in the TEl region). This result is a compromise between the degree of tempering of the initial martensitic microstructure and the amount of transformed martensite.

The results show that the highest plastic properties were obtained for samples soaked at 680 °C for 15 and 60 min (UEl >17% and TEl >24%); further increase in soaking time results in decrease of UTS, TEl, UEl and hardness values.

To better describe the microstructure-property relationships in the investigated samples, interrupted tensile tests were performed. The tests were performed for samples soaked for 1 min, 15 and 300 min, as characterized by a differentiated fraction of RA, its stability and the obtained mechanical properties. After reaching the set strain for each sample ( Fig. 6 
                         ), the tensile test was stopped and a piece of material was cut from the test area, subjected to a typical surface preparation procedure, and then the RA content was determined by XRD method. The obtained results showing changes in the fraction of RA in a given sample as a function of true strain ( Fig. 6 a) were compared with the calculations of

As indicated earlier by the theoretical calculations in  Fig. 4 b, the stability of the RA decreases with an increase in soaking time, due to C and Mn partitioning and grain size increase. The calculated RA stability for different samples has a direct reflection in the measured changes in its fraction with the increase of strain in the interrupted tensile tests ( Fig. 6 a). The standard deviation values of the XRD measurements are lower than 4% for all samples, indicating a uniform transformation range of RA in a given area of the sample. In the UEl range the fraction of RA in the sample soaked for 1 min is almost constant; it changes from an initial 16 to 14% at strain of UEl. The transformation rate (TR), which is the fraction of RA transformed per given strain, averages 0.2% RA for 0.01 of the true strain in the range of UEl for this sample. For the sample soaked for 15 min, the decrease in RA fraction is the most gradual with the progress of strain among all samples. TR averages 0.9% RA to 0.01 of true strain in the range of UEl. For the sample soaked for 300 min, the SIMT is very dynamic up to true strain of 0.05 (TR is 4.6% RA for 0.01 true strain), and next slows down to 1.2% RA for 0.01 of true strain up to true strain of 0.09, and to 0.5% RA for 0.01 of true strain up to true strain of 0.15.

Regardless of the initial fraction and stability of RA after heat treatment presented in  Fig. 4 , the UEl regions of the tensile samples contain at least 10% of RA ( Fig. 4 c). The most significant reason for this phenomenon is the evolution of grain size during plastic deformation, as the second factor controlling RA stability – its chemical composition – can be considered constant at RT. As indicated by SEM ( Fig. 1 ) and EBSD ( Fig. 2 ) results, tensile deformation results in intensive fragmentation of RA, which was also observed in a similar study by Luo et al., [ 35 ]. The post-deformation average grain sizes of RA in all samples do not exceed 0.015 μm 3 . To describe the phenomena in greater detail, the distributions of the lengths of the minor and major axes of RA grains (determined by the EBSD method) for undeformed and deformed samples were plotted for selected samples in  Fig. 8 
                         . One can see that before deformation, both major and minor axes of RA grains in the sample soaked at 680 °C for 1 min were the shortest among all samples ( Fig. 8 a and c). In this sample, the peak length is less than 0.5 μm for the major axis and about 0.1 μm for the minor axis. As the soaking time increases, the frequency of larger grains increases. For the sample annealed for 300 min, for the minor axis, the frequency peak occurs at a length of about 0.2 μm and is 0.24, for longer grains the frequency slightly decreases, but for the length of 2 μm it still exceeds 0.1. For the minor axis, the distribution is also more gradual, and the frequency peak of 0.24 is observed for the length of about 0.22 μm. After tensile deformation, the distribution of both axes becomes very similar, regardless of the sample. The size of the RA reaches some critical level, which is common for different samples. The length of major axis for majority of grains is below 0.5 μm and the peak length of minor axis for all samples is about 0.1 μm. The tendency to achieve a given critical size of RA during strain was also indicated by the post-deformation average volume of RA after deformation presented in  Fig. 4 a.

The above-mentioned results indicate that if the RA grain refinement, and its chemical composition are considered as separate factors, the former would be stronger limiting the range of the SIMT effect. However, these factors overlap because smaller grains of austenite tend to contain a higher C and Mn content as the diffusion path is shorter and solutes in parent martensite are divided into smaller volumes ( Table 2 ). Therefore, the shortest IA produces the most stable RA, due to the smallest size and the highest enrichment in C.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs:
The effect of mechanical stability of RA, especially considering the grain size effect, was systematically studied in this paper. The main findings are as follows. 
                         
                            • 
                            The stress-induced martensite start temperature ( 
                                  
                                     
                                        M 
                                        s 
                                        σ 
                                     
                                  
                               ) of retained austenite (RA) below −100 °C, arising from the chemical composition and presence of ultra-fine RA grains, hinders the occurrence of strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) effect in the sample soaked for 1 min at 680 °C. As a consequence, the strain hardening capability is low and the total elongation (TEl) reaches only 13.5% for this sample. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The increase in RA fraction is accompanied by decrease of its stability. The plasticity level follows an increasing RA fraction to some point (32% of RA characterized by average  
                                  
                                     
                                        M 
                                        s 
                                        σ 
                                     
                                  
                                temperature of −24 °C), after which the low RA stability caused by overgrown grains cause the intense SIMT effect to take place in early strain stage resulting in limited uniform elongation (UEl) values. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Better plasticity may be obtained in the steel containing less RA but characterized by optimized mechanical stability. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            For the high plastic properties of medium-Mn steels, a compromise between the chemical composition and the grain size distribution of RA is needed to generate the wide range of RA stability, ensuring gradual SIMT transformation. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The influence of grain size on the stability range of RA exhibits a non-linear tendency. It is important to note that even with a similar distribution of grain sizes, varying the average grain size will yield different effects on the stability range of RA.
